source: Fleming & Lau (2014) How to measure metacognition
finding: Defines three separate ideas: metacognitive bias (overall confidence level), metacognitive sensitivity (how well confidence separates own correct from incorrect trials) and metacognitive efficiency (sensitivity given task performance). Pearson phi and Goodman-Kruskal gamma are contaminated by bias and by task performance.
numbers: No single experiment; a measurement review. Type 2 AUROC of 0.5 is chance.
quote: the same individual will appear to have greater metacognitive sensitivity on an easy task compared to a hard task
limits: Gamma and phi are popular in memory research but shift with how often a person says 'high confidence', so they can mislead.
agent_relevance: Measure the agent's stated confidence with a bias-free sensitivity score (AUROC or meta-d'), never with raw correlation or average confidence alone. Report bias, sensitivity and calibration as three separate numbers.

source: Fleming & Lau (2014) How to measure metacognition (type 2 SDT section)
finding: Type 2 hit rate is the share of high-confidence trials among correct trials; type 2 false alarm rate is the share among incorrect trials. The type 2 ROC traces these two across criteria. Parametric type 2 d' is unsafe because type 2 distributions are unequal-variance and non-Gaussian (Galvin 2003); Evans & Azzopardi (2007) showed in simulation that type 2 d' is confounded by bias.
numbers: Area under type 2 ROC (AUROC2) = 0.5 at chance.
limits: AUROC2 is non-parametric but still rises with task accuracy, so it cannot compare a strong and a weak model fairly.
agent_relevance: When comparing two LLMs or two prompts, AUROC2 alone favours the more accurate one. Use an accuracy-adjusted measure or compare at matched accuracy.

source: Fleming & Lau (2014) How to measure metacognition (meta-d' section)
finding: meta-d' (Maniscalco & Lau 2012) is the type 1 d' that an ideal observer would need to produce the observed confidence ratings. It is in the same units as d', so meta-d'/d' (M-ratio) is a performance-controlled efficiency score. Barrett et al. (2013) normative tests found it robust to bias changes and able to recover simulated sensitivity changes.
numbers: M-ratio 1 = ideal use of the available evidence; below 1 = noisy confidence; above 1 possible when confidence uses extra information.
limits: Assumes Gaussian equal-variance SDT at type 1; needs ratings across several confidence levels and many trials.
agent_relevance: A guardrail test for the agent: compute M-ratio on a fixed set of problems so a change in prompt cannot look better just by solving more items.

source: Fleming (2017) HMeta-d: hierarchical Bayesian estimation of metacognitive efficiency from confidence ratings
finding: Hierarchical Bayesian version of meta-d'. It estimates M-ratio per subject with group-level priors, gives credible intervals, avoids edge-correction confounds and does better than separate point fits when data are few. Simulations show the advantage with limited data, e.g. patient groups.
numbers: Output is a posterior over log M-ratio; 95% credible interval or HDI used for group tests. Exact simulation sizes not recorded here.
limits: Meta-d' can exceed d' when people use hunches, post-decision evidence or knowledge of other influences. Cross-domain correlations of efficiency are mixed (modest in Ais 2016, McCurdy 2013; absent in Baird 2013, Kelemen 2000).
agent_relevance: With few graded trials per task type, use pooled or hierarchical estimates; point estimates of confidence quality from a small set are unstable.

source: Fleming & Daw (2017) Self-evaluation of decision-making: a general Bayesian framework for metacognitive computation
finding: Core model: confidence is a second-order inference. A separate but coupled system estimates the probability that the first-order decision was correct, like judging another actor. First-order models use one internal state for both decision and confidence. The second-order model also uses the agent's own action as evidence, and accounts for confidence, error detection and post-decision change in one frame.
numbers: Simulation paper (code on GitHub). Confidence z = P(action = world state | confidence variable). In the post-decisional variant X_conf = X_act + X_new.
quote: People are often aware of their mistakes, and report levels of confidence in their choices that correlate with objective performance.
limits: Model evidence is mostly simulation and re-reading of earlier findings, not a new large human dataset. Distinguishing second-order from post-decisional first-order accounts needs specific designs.
agent_relevance: Design implication: the checker of an answer should be a separate pass that sees the answer and its own evidence, not the same forward pass that produced it. This matches schema G2/G4 (do not let a model grade its own text unaided).

source: Fleming & Daw (2017), dissociations section
finding: Lists why confidence and accuracy can come apart: extra noise in the read-out of confidence, evidence that arrives after the decision, and evidence inaccessible to the decision (error detection with the error-related negativity, Gehring 1993; blindsight, Weiskrantz 1974). Second-order computation lets metacognition be better or worse than task performance.
numbers: Qualitative review of Rabbitt 1966, Rabbitt & Rodgers 1977, Baranski & Petrusic 1998/2001, Del Cul 2009 and others.
limits: Cited findings are from varied paradigms; not one pooled estimate.
agent_relevance: Confidence can legitimately improve with more processing after the answer (a re-check), but it can also be noisier than the answer itself; do not assume stated confidence is a free readout.

source: Nelson & Narens (1990) Metamemory: a theoretical framework and new findings
finding: Two-level architecture: an object level (doing the task) and a meta level (a model of the object level). Monitoring is information flowing up (confidence, feeling of knowing, judgments of learning); control is flow down (stop, continue, allocate study time, search strategy).
numbers: Not opened this session; description from standard citation knowledge. No numbers recorded.
limits: Conceptual framework; later work (Koriat) showed monitoring is inferential, built from cues.
agent_relevance: Maps directly onto our program/model split: the model works at object level, the program holds the meta level (counts, checks, budget) and decides stop or continue.

source: Koriat (1997) Monitoring one's own knowledge during study: a cue-utilization approach to judgments of learning
finding: Judgments of learning are inferences from cues (intrinsic item difficulty, extrinsic study conditions, mnemonic cues such as retrieval fluency), not direct reads of memory trace strength. Cues can mislead, for example fluency.
numbers: Not opened this session; no numbers recorded.
limits: Later work (Koriat 2012) proposes self-consistency across internally generated answers as the basis of confidence.
agent_relevance: Stated confidence from an LLM is likely also a cue-based guess (fluency, length, familiarity). Prefer signals tied to behaviour: agreement of samples, check results.

source: Maniscalco & Lau (2012) A signal detection theoretic approach for estimating metacognitive sensitivity from confidence ratings
finding: Introduced meta-d'. The method fits the type 2 ROC given the type 1 SDT model, so metacognitive sensitivity is expressed in type 1 d' units.
numbers: Not opened this session; behaviour of the measure is described via Fleming & Lau 2014 (opened).
limits: Equal-variance Gaussian assumption at type 1.
agent_relevance: Source of the efficiency measure the guardrail can use.

source: Fleming, Weil, Nagy, Dolan & Rees (2010) Relating introspective accuracy to individual differences in brain structure
finding: Healthy adults differed reliably in how well confidence tracked accuracy on a perceptual task while first-order performance was held about constant by a staircase. Better introspective accuracy went with more grey matter in anterior prefrontal cortex and with white-matter microstructure there.
numbers: From memory of the paper (about 32 participants); not opened, numbers unverified.
limits: Correlational, one task. Later work (Baird 2013, 2015) found metacognitive ability for memory and perception depends on partly distinct networks.
agent_relevance: Metacognitive skill is a separate ability from task skill, so a stronger solver model is not guaranteed to be a better judge of itself.

source: Pouget, Drugowitsch & Kepecs (2016) Confidence and certainty: distinct probabilistic quantities for different goals
finding: Separates confidence (probability a choice is correct, given the evidence and the choice) from certainty (precision of the belief about the stimulus). They can come apart.
numbers: Not opened this session; no numbers recorded.
limits: Conceptual; argues that some neural findings equate the two.
agent_relevance: Our guardrail must say which one is meant. 'How sure am I the answer is right' (confidence) is the useful quantity; 'how peaked is my token distribution' is not the same thing.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Language models (mostly) know what they know
finding: Large models are well calibrated on multiple-choice questions when the answer options are visible with letters (BIG-bench, MMLU and others). Calibration improves with model size and from 0-shot to few-shot. Within BIG-bench they found no clear link between accuracy and calibration across tasks.
numbers: Anthropic models up to 52B; ECE with 10 equal-mass bins. Replacing one option with 'none of the above' reduced both accuracy and calibration significantly.
quote: larger models are well-calibrated on diverse multiple choice and true/false questions when they are provided in the right format
limits: Format-dependent: calibration depends on seeing the options first. Pretrained models, not the final RLHF chat models.
agent_relevance: Do not assume that good calibration on multiple choice carries over to free text. Test the agent's confidence in the exact answer format it will use.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022), P(True) self-evaluation
finding: Models can judge their own sampled answers as True/False (P(True)). It is harder than judging fixed questions because models find their own samples more plausible. Few-shot self-evaluation is calibrated; zero-shot is not. Showing the model many of its own T=1 samples plus the one to judge improves the judgment. More shots mainly help calibration, not AUROC.
numbers: Tasks: TriviaQA, Lambada, GSM8k, HumanEval, arithmetic, GitHub function synthesis.
quote: models tend to find their own samples more plausible
limits: Not a causal test; the sampled-answer context acts like a self-consistency signal.
agent_relevance: Supports a program-run vote (many samples shown together) over a single 'are you sure?' check. It also matches schema G4: agreement is a hint, not proof.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022), P(IK) and RLHF temperature
finding: A head trained to predict 'do I know this' (P(IK)) works for in-distribution questions and partly generalises, but is poorly calibrated on new tasks. P(IK) rises when relevant source text or hints are in context. RLHF policies look miscalibrated but become fairly well calibrated with a simple temperature adjustment on several evaluations.
numbers: 52B classifiers; AUROC and Brier tables compare training on TriviaQA only vs everything. Column labels were garbled in text extraction, so exact per-task values are not recorded.
limits: Needs labelled training data; out-of-domain calibration weak.
agent_relevance: A learned 'will I solve this' gate is plausible but needs retraining per domain; do not trust it zero-shot on new problem types.

source: Lin, Hilton & Evans (2022) Teaching models to express their uncertainty in words
finding: First demonstration that GPT-3 (175B) can be fine-tuned to state its own confidence in words or percentages that are calibrated, without using logits. It stays moderately calibrated under distribution shift and tracks real uncertainty rather than copying human examples. Verbalised and logit-based methods both generalise.
numbers: CalibratedMath: 21 arithmetic tasks. Train on Add-subtract (median accuracy 21%), test on Multi-answer (median accuracy 65%) and Multiply-divide. Compared to a constant baseline; 100 questions sampled per sub-task for labels.
quote: the model remains moderately calibrated under distribution shift
limits: Only GPT-3 175B and only arithmetic. Fine-tuned on the model's own accuracy per sub-task, so it may learn task-type difficulty rather than item-level knowledge.
agent_relevance: Verbal confidence can be trained in, but if the signal is just task-type difficulty it is weak at ranking items within a type; check item-level AUROC.

source: Tian et al. (2023) Just ask for calibration: strategies for eliciting calibrated confidence scores from language models fine-tuned with human feedback
finding: For RLHF chat models (ChatGPT, GPT-4, Claude 2), confidence the model writes out as a number is usually better calibrated than its token probabilities on TriviaQA, SciQ and TruthfulQA, often cutting ECE by a relative 50% or more. Asking for several candidate answers with probabilities (a 'consider the opposite' step) helps further. Token probabilities from these models are overconfident.
numbers: ECE and ECE after temperature scaling, Brier score and AUC reported per model and dataset; n=10 samples used for the consistency baseline.
quote: verbalized confidences emitted as output tokens are typically better-calibrated than the model's conditional probabilities
limits: Calibration (ECE) improved; discrimination (AUC) stays modest. A model that always says 50% can have good ECE, so ECE alone hides low sensitivity.
agent_relevance: Ask for a verbal number, but pair it with a rank-based score such as AUROC, and add a check that does not depend on the number.

source: Xiong et al. (2024) Can LLMs express their uncertainty? An empirical evaluation of confidence elicitation in LLMs (ICLR)
finding: Black-box study with GPT-3, GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Vicuna and LLaMA-2 Chat on eight tasks. Verbalised confidence is overconfident, probably because it copies human patterns of expressing confidence. Calibration and failure prediction improve with model scale. Vanilla verbalised confidence has poor failure prediction even for GPT-4.
numbers: Vanilla verbal ECE above 0.377 average for GPT-3, GPT-3.5 and Vicuna; GPT-4 average AUROC only 62.7% (chance 50%); about 22.2% AUROC improvement from GPT-3 to GPT-4.
quote: LLMs, when verbalizing their confidence, tend to be overconfident, potentially imitating human patterns of expressing confidence.
limits: Black-box elicitation only; a professional-knowledge task set (law, ethics) stays hard for all methods. No method wins everywhere.
agent_relevance: Do not use a model's stated confidence alone to trigger or skip checks; AUROC near 0.6 is close to useless as a gate.

source: Xiong et al. (2024), prompting and sampling strategies
finding: Human-inspired prompts (e.g. chain-of-thought, top-K guesses) reduce ECE but do not fix failure prediction; AUROC stays close to random guessing. High accuracy can give low ECE just by outputting 100% for everything. Sampling several answers and using their agreement is much better: GSM8K AUROC rose from 54.8% (verbalised) to 92.7% (5 samples with consistency).
numbers: GPT-4 on GSM8K: 93.6% accuracy; near-optimal ECE 0.064 by assigning 100% confidence to all samples. Best aggregation reached ECE 0.028. White-box vs black-box gap in AUROC: 0.522 to 0.605.
limits: Consistency is costly (5-13 samples) and weaker where answers are free-form or where all samples share the same error.
agent_relevance: Best evidence that agreement across samples beats self-reported confidence for gating, while G4 reminds us that samples from one model share errors. Use agreement as a trigger only.

source: Kapoor et al. (2024) Large language models must be taught to know what they don't know (NeurIPS)
finding: Prompting alone gives poorly calibrated uncertainty, and calibration (ECE) does not improve as the base model gets better. Fine-tuning on graded correct and incorrect answers (LoRA) does. About 1000 graded examples beat baselines; gains continue to about 5000 then flatten. Estimators partly transfer across models, and can estimate other models' uncertainty. Sampling methods calibrate but discriminate weakly; verbal elicitation discriminates fairly but calibrates badly.
numbers: Open models (LLaMA-2, Mistral) on open-ended and multiple-choice MMLU. User study N=181 with Mistral 7B Instruct: participants used reliable confidence scores to decide when to agree with the model, and ignored a random-score control.
limits: Needs labelled data per domain and white-box access for the best methods (LoRA + probe). The user study was preliminary.
agent_relevance: A small graded set (about 1000 items) from our own task type could train a cheap confidence head; for a closed API model it is not available, so use agreement plus real checks.

source: Steyvers et al. (2025) What large language models know and what people think they know (Nature Machine Intelligence)
finding: Calibration gap and discrimination gap: people who read default LLM explanations over-trust them. The LLM's own confidence discriminates correct from incorrect (GPT-3.5 AUC .751, PaLM2 .746, GPT-4o short answer .781), but participants reading explanations reached only about .59-.60. Longer explanations raised user confidence with no gain in accuracy. Matching the explanation's wording to the model's internal confidence narrowed both gaps.
numbers: 301 participants across Experiments 1 and 2 (284 retained for analysis), 40 questions each; questions: 350 (GPT-3.5, PaLM2 accuracy 55% and 50%) and 336 (GPT-4o accuracy 63%). Human AUC: .589 (GPT-3.5), .602 (PaLM2), .592 (GPT-4o). Bayes factors above 100 for low vs medium vs high confidence wording.
quote: users tend to overestimate the accuracy of LLM responses when provided with default explanations
limits: Short multiple-choice and short-answer trivia; US online sample; effect of explanation style measured on trust, not on final decision quality.
agent_relevance: What the agent says about confidence must be consistent with its measured reliability, and the final text should not carry extra length that inflates reader trust.

source: Steyvers & Peters (2025) Metacognition and uncertainty communication in humans and large language models
finding: Review that sets LLM confidence against human metacognition measures (sensitivity, calibration, efficiency). Example: GPT-3.5 token-based MMLU confidence is overconfident (AUC .778); a confidence-fine-tuned GPT-4.1-mini on TriviaQA reached AUC .83 with better calibration. Notes that LLMs and humans are both overconfident (Cash et al. 2025) but that study used AUROC2, which is confounded with accuracy. Sample-consistency confidence in LLMs parallels Koriat's (2012) self-consistency account of human confidence.
numbers: AUC .778 (GPT-3.5, MMLU, logits) vs .83 (GPT-4.1-mini, fine-tuned, TriviaQA).
quote: consistency across internally simulated alternatives may serve as a basis for confidence
limits: Narrative review; most LLM studies cited do not control accuracy when comparing metacognitive sensitivity.
agent_relevance: Use meta-d' style controls in our own tests so that a stronger model is not credited with better introspection just for being more accurate.

source: Kumaran, Fleming et al. (2025) How overconfidence in initial choices and underconfidence under criticism modulate change of mind in LLMs
finding: Using a two-turn paradigm borrowed from human confidence research, but with the initial answer hidden or shown (impossible with humans), Gemma 3, GPT-4o and o1-preview show choice-supportive bias: when their earlier answer is visible they change their mind much less. They also overweight opposing advice compared with a Bayesian observer.
numbers: Mean change-of-mind rate 32.5% (answer hidden) vs 13.1% (answer shown); display-type regression coefficient -3.4, p<0.0001. With opposite advice, change rate 39.2% (shown) vs 85.0% (hidden). Opposing advice update was 2.58 times the Bayesian update; supporting advice only 1.095 times. Temperature for calibration set at 3.3.
quote: a drive to maintain consistency with prior commitments and hypersensitivity to contradictory feedback
limits: Tasks include a latitude estimation set, SimpleQA (chance 25%, accuracy 40.5%) and GSM-MC; advice quality varied from 50% to 100% accuracy.
agent_relevance: Two failure modes for a revise loop at once: sticking to the first answer when it is visible and over-reacting to any contradiction. Supports G2: revise from a real failing output, and keep the first answer hidden when asking for a fresh confidence.

source: Luo & Jho (2026) Predictive metacognition: a neuro-computational framework for self-monitoring in LLMs (Scientific Reports)
finding: LoRA fine-tuning (rank 8, alpha 16, 4000 examples across confidence levels) of Llama-3-8B-Instruct and Phi-3-Mini to output an answer and a confidence. Reported lower Brier score (11.6% and 17.2%) and ECE than base models, with a small accuracy gain.
numbers: Llama-3-8B: accuracy 0.853 vs 0.837 base; Brier 0.122 vs 0.138; ECE 0.224 vs 0.252. Phi-3-Mini: accuracy 0.847, Brier 0.128, ECE 0.231. Base Llama after temperature scaling: ECE 0.107 (n=250 held-out), Brier 0.211, conformal coverage 0.996.
limits: The base model after a simple temperature fit (ECE 0.107) beats the fine-tuned metacognitive model (ECE 0.224) in the paper's own table, so the headline gain is against an uncalibrated baseline. Small model, small data, 'neuro-inspired' framing is mostly naming.
agent_relevance: Treat claims of brain-inspired metacognition modules sceptically; always compare with temperature scaling or a held-out recalibration.

source: Dunning & Kruger (1999) Unskilled and unaware of it
finding: Low scorers in humour, logic and grammar tests overestimated their percentile; top scorers slightly underestimated. Claimed that the skill needed to do a task is also needed to judge it.
numbers: Not opened this session; numbers not recorded here.
limits: Debated: statistical regression to the mean and better-than-average effects can reproduce much of the pattern (Krueger & Mueller 2002; Nuhfer et al. 2016).
agent_relevance: Cautionary: a weak solver may be unable to tell its answers are wrong. Do not give a weak model the job of vetoing itself.

source: Griot et al. (2025) Large language models lack essential metacognition for reliable medical reasoning (Nature Communications)
finding: A medical benchmark with 'none of the above' and uncertainty items found frontier LLMs often confident when wrong. Cited here as a pointer to be read in the second pass.
numbers: Not opened this session; no numbers recorded.
limits: Details unverified by me.
agent_relevance: Pointer for Angle B: test our guardrail on an unanswerable-item set.
